lines.markdown: Customers will tell you a dark roast is *stronger*. Before you agree, see what the roast really changes.

items.title: Light roast
items.alt: A pile of light brown, dry-looking beans.
items.markdown: Dropped soon after first crack. The coffee keeps the taste of its origin and process: fruit, flowers, a bright acidity. Most of our pour-overs are light.

items.title: Medium roast
items.alt: A pile of medium brown beans.
items.markdown: A little longer: the acidity softens and caramel and nuts come forward. A balanced cup that suits most customers.

items.title: Medium-dark roast
items.alt: A pile of dark brown beans with a few shiny spots.
items.markdown: Near the second crack, oil starts to show on the beans. Chocolate and spice take over from fruit, and the body grows heavier.

items.title: Dark roast
items.alt: A pile of almost black, oily beans.
items.markdown: Shiny with oil, close to black. The roast's smoky, bitter taste covers the origin: two very different coffees end up tasting alike.

props.text: Myths you will hear at the counter

props.prompt: Before you turn each card, decide: myth or fact?

items.title: Dark roast has more caffeine
items.markdown: Myth. Roasting barely changes the caffeine. A dark bean is lighter, so a scoop of dark beans may even hold a little less. A strong taste is not strength.

items.title: Beans keep best in the fridge
items.markdown: Myth. A fridge is damp and full of smells that beans soak up. Keep them airtight, cool and dark, and use them within a few weeks.

items.title: Espresso is a kind of bean
items.markdown: Myth. Espresso is a way of brewing: hot water pushed through fine grounds under pressure. Any bean can make an espresso; roasters choose the ones that taste best that way.

items.title: The fresher the roast, the better
items.markdown: Not quite. Beans need a few days to let out their gas after roasting. After that, they are at their best for a few weeks.

props.alt: A single roasted coffee bean, seen large, its centre cut running down the middle.
props.prompt: Read a roasted bean as a roaster does.

items.title: The centre cut
items.markdown: Where the two seeds faced each other in the cherry. A cut much paler than the rest of the bean can mean it was roasted too fast.

items.title: Chaff
items.markdown: Flakes of silverskin caught in the cut. Most of it blows away in the roaster; what stays is harmless.

items.title: Oil
items.markdown: Oil on the surface means a dark roast, or beans roasted long ago. A light roast should look dry.

items.title: The colour
items.markdown: An even brown: a medium roast. Roasters measure the colour with a meter, to roast each batch the same.

props.stem: A customer loves the berry notes of our natural Ethiopia. Which roast keeps them best?

options.text: A dark roast, so the notes come out stronger
options.feedback: A dark roast covers the origin with its own smoky taste: the berries would be the first thing to go.

options.text: A light roast, dropped soon after first crack
options.feedback: Yes: a light roast keeps the fruit of the origin and of the natural process.

options.text: A medium-dark roast, for more body
options.feedback: More body, but chocolate and spice take over from the fruit at that level.

props.prompt: How sure do you feel explaining to a customer what the roast changes, and what it does not?

props.alt: Three cups of coffee on a dark counter, from amber to almost black.
props.markdown: Roast changes a coffee's flavour far more than its caffeine.
